WEDNESDAY, 26 JUNE 2013
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.
Prayers.
Prime Minister—Government Communications Security Bureau Legislation and
Auckland City Rail Link
1. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes. I particularly stand by my statement
that was what a ripper of a front page the New Zealand Herald had this morning.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he stand by his statement: “They might have to ask themselves
if one day there was an equivalent of the Boston bombings in New Zealand, would they
be the very same members who would stand up and say they prevented New Zealanders
from being kept as safe as they otherwise could be.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, and I think I can recall al so the Rt Hon Winston Peters
making very similar comments on television last night.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Has he seen evidence or intelligence that New Zealanders have been
at risk of physical or terrorist attack over the last 12 months; if so, what action has he
taken?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It is not in the public interest for me to outline—[Interruption]
It is not in the public  interest for me to outline all the threats that New Zealand might
face or the intelligence that we gather, but I think I can say at a broad level as the
Minister responsible and as Prime Minister  that the agencies do collectively actively
collect information to protect New Zealand. I think New Zealanders  would expect that.
That is why when Helen Clark was Prime Minister she did exactly what this law is
proposing to do.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: In quoting the Boston bombings, is he talking about a real or urgent
threat based on evidence, or is he merely scaremongering to get his legislation across
the line?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The legislation that is bei ng proposed under the Government
Communications Security Bureau, as the member  knows, is for the bur eau to be able to
continue to provide agency support with better supervision to our other agencies like the
police, the SIS, and the Defence Force. It does so because from time to time it has
concerns about individuals or  groups who might pose a threat  to New Zealand. If that
member seriously wants to get up in this H ouse and try to make himself feel better for
taking the position that Grant Robertson has forced down his throat—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! That is a sufficient answer to that
question.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: At least the polling is not going down as fast as—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! Would the Hon Tau Henare cease from
displaying that particular piece of paper. [ Interruption] Order! I say to the Hon Tau
Henare that if this continues, I will ask him to leave the Chamber.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Given his citing of the Boston bo mbings and the perceived possible
threat to the physical well-be ing of New Zealanders, why di d he not therefore move as
soon as he could last year to bring in urgent legislation to keep New Zealanders safe?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: As the member knows, we did act  as quickly as we could to
have a thorough review of the Government Communications Security Bureau so that we
could understand completely all of the issues and could pro pose legislation that would
11266 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Jun 2013
fully reflect what was required. We have now actually determined what is required, and,
actually, the member is looking for a way to get out of his position. I would just say one
thing to him, and it is this—and this is  rather spooky: Mighty River Power is up 5.5
percent today, and that is the same number that Labour has lost in the polls.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Why is he performing such a sp ectacular U-turn on the Auckland
City Rail Link when he has previously said that “the advice that we’ve had is that it
doesn’t stack up.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: What the Government is going to be announcing on Friday is
that it will be supporting the construction of the central bus iness district rail loop, and
on a slower start date than the one propos ed by the council. That will be 2020. The
Government will make a contribution, and that is because as a Government we will also
be announcing integrated projects that s upport the infrastructure  of Auckland, and,
again, maybe that is why we are polling 49 percent and Labour is polling 30 percent.
We are thinking about what is  important to New Zealand, a nd Labour is constantly in
the gutter, with nothing decent to talk about.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is he therefore confirming that he and his Government have changed
their position on the Auckland City Rail Li nk, in line with Labour Party long-held
policy?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, it is not for me to understand Labour’s policies,
although I showed in the last campaign that I understood them better than Phil Goff did,
but, putting that all to one side, no, I do not th ink it is on the same time frame. We are
suggesting a start date of 2020. I do not think that is what Labour is proposing.
Economy—Debt Levels
2. PAUL GOLDSMITH (National)  to the Minister of Finance : What progress is
the Government making to ensure future generations of New Zealanders are not saddled
with excessive debt?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Government is making
significant progress in getting debt under cont rol. It is important to remember the
situation inherited by the Na tional-led Government in 2008.  Back then, Treasury was
forecasting never-ending fiscal deficits a nd Government debt rising, roughly, for ever,
and at the time the current account deficit was above 8.8 percent of GDP. That situation
was clearly unsustainable. The Government ha s taken decisive action over five Budgets
to get its own books back to surplus by 2014- 15, to start repaying debt, and to help
bring the current account deficit down from those previously high levels.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: As part of its wider programme, what progress is the Government
making in getting its own books in order?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Budget forecasts show net core Crown debt peaking at 28.7
percent of GDP in 2014-15 be fore declining. Longer-term pr ojections show net debt
dropping to 17.6 percent of GDP by 2020-21. Proj ections in 2009 indica ted that if the
Government had maintained the spending track it inherited, net debt would likely
exceed 60 percent of GDP by the early 2020s. Government decisions since then mean
that net Government debt will be around 40 percent of GDP lower than projected. That
is a difference of more than $80 billion—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am concerned about the
member opposite, who continues to undermine your ruling by displaying the card with
his IQ on it across the House there.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I was unaware that the member was continuing to use that, but if it
is raised again, Hon Tau Henare, you will leave the Chamber.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: I seek leave to table—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No.
26 Jun 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 11267

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: —the No. 30.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will please leave the Chamber for the balance
of question time.
Hon Tau Henare withdrew from the Chamber.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Have we got a supplementary question?

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Can I ask the Minister—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am sorry; I have a point of order from Gerry Brownlee.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I fully accept the ruling
that you have just made, but I would ask that when all sorts of signage and other such is
displayed on a future occasion by the Oppos ition, a similar appro ach will be taken,
because it is equally offensive at various times.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No, there is no need for any further comment. Mr Henare
was asked to not show that a ny further, and he continued to  do so. That is defying the
Speaker.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What reports—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Before that last point
of order, you had indicated that it was going to be my question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No. I determine when I take supplementary questions and from
where I take them. I did at one  stage think the member was raising a point of order. The
member tends to stand to his feet and not a nnounce to me whether it is a supplementary
question he is seeking or a point of order, which does not make it helpful.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am happy to look at
the Parliamentary record, but, with respect, that  is balderdash. I get to my feet and I ask
a supplementary question or I make a point of order, and that sort of criticism will not
do.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And I have accepted a supplementary question from Paul
Goldsmith. I will come to the member in due time.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What reports has he received on New Zealand’s wider national
debt position, particularly with respect to the current account and the net international
investment position?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Statistics New Zealand last week reported the March
quarter data on both the current account and New Zealand’s net international investment
position. This showed that the current account deficit narrowed slightly, to 4.8 percent
of GDP as at 31 March, down from 5 percent as at 31 December. New Zealand has run
current account deficits for around 40 years, but the situation became extremely serious
in 2006, 2007, and 2008, when the deficit was consistently higher than 8 percent of
GDP. The net international debt position also improved a little in the March quarter: it
fell to 69.3 percent of GDP, dow n from 71.4 percent in December. Although that is still
high, it compares favourably w ith the net interna tional debt position of 85 percent of
GDP in early 2009.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How does the Minister reconcile  that last answer and the
one before that with a current account deficit of $10 billion, heading towards $17
billion—every dollar of which is debt—and the worst borrowing re cord in over 70
years?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I cannot agree with the member’s statements, and I think
the first issue is that he is looking at amount s, rather than at pe rcentages of GDP. Of
course, if you have a larger GDP, then you can  actually have a larg er amount of debt—
which may be relevant to the member in future. But in te rms of the current account, the
actual percentage of GDP has actually declined, which is the key point, from 8.5 percent
or more of GDP in 2008 down to around 4.8 percent now. That is good progress.
11268 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Jun 2013

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What contributions are manuf acturers making in helping New
Zealand build economic growth?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: A very good question. Manufacturers are making a
significant contribution. Since the beginni ng of 2009 the manufacturing sector has
grown by 9.2 percent. That is a very  significant turn-round from 2008, when
manufacturing shrank by 12 percent in just 1 year. Since 2009—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: How much of that’s non-primary sector?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —wait and it will come, “Mr Parrot”—non-food
manufacturing sales have grown by 6.3 percen t. In 2008 they fell by 7.2 percent. Since
2009 non-food manufacturing volumes have grow n by 1.3 percent. In 2008 they fell by
nearly 15 percent, and non-food manufacturin g export volumes have grown by nearly
15 percent since 2009. Finally, of cour se, the manufacturing BNZ-Business New
Zealand Performance of Manufacturing Index is currently at 59.2, compared to 35.8 in

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Given the Minister did not know the answer to that question
yesterday, can he now confirm that manufact uring exports outside the primary sector
are down in real terms by 17 percent since 2008 and by 6 percent in the last full year for
which there are records?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I have checked and, no, I cannot, because the figures I have
just quoted—the non-food manufacturing—is the closest information. I appreciate the
member may have constructed his own series in terms of reducing it. The other thing is
that Mr Parker seems to be trying to use th e CPI to deflate the export figures, hence his
use of what he calls real terms. Of course , that is simply wrong, as domestic CPI is not
the way to deflate export prices and volumes. So, I am sorry, but Mr Parker is just being
a wee bit too tricky with these numbers.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is it correct that, according to the Reserve Bank, the level of
borrowing for residential housing is at an al l-time high of $181 billion; if so, how much
additional debt does he expect New Zealande rs will take on to buy houses over the next
year, with house price inflation in Auckland currently running at 15 percent?

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: At half what it was under Labour.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, exactly. I think that record is significantly better than
under the Labour Government. I think the issue—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My question was whether
the figure that I gave is correct. It was not what the Minister—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I heard the question, and if we could give the Minister an
opportunity to answer, then I will decide whether it has been addressed.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, I do not have the exact numbers and, given I have
just been deconstructing the member’s previ ous question, I am rather leery as to his
numbers.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. He says he does not know
the answer to that question, so I am happy with that answer.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I heard that, but that is not a le gitimate point of order. We are going
to have difficulty—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. If the purpose of question
time is for the Minister to address the questi on and the Minister says: “I don’t have that
information.”, it is not within his ambit to address another question that was not asked.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I would—[ Interruption] Order! No, I do not need any
assistance. The difficulty I want to see ceas e is a situation where any member asks a
question, then decides they ar e either unhappy with the answer  or completely satisfied
with the answer, and then raises a point of or der that stops a Minister from finishing the
answer to the Minister’s satisfaction. If th at continues to happen, the best way forward
26 Jun 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 11269
for me is to then move to the next question, because I will assume on that basis that the
person who has asked the question is completely  satisfied with the answer. Therefore, I
see the opportunity for the fo rfeiture of supplementary que stions. I do not want to do
that. There will be the odd occasion when it is legitimate for a member to say the
question has gone on—[Interruption] Order! I am trying to help  the House, particularly
after yesterday. But we are going to get into difficulty if whenever a member thinks he
or she has heard enough, he or sh e raises a point of order to say: “That’s sufficient, let’s
move on.”

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. In the previous Speaker’s
term we got into the rhythm in this Hous e that if a straight  question was asked, a
straight answer would come b ack. The issue that we on this side of the House have is
that when we ask a question that is a stra ightforward question, th e Minister says: “I
don’t have that information.”, and then proceed s to go into either a political attack or
some other thing. That is where the difficult y lies for us. We woul d like to see that
ruling continue to be in force, and then we will not have the problems that you are
suggesting.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will—

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Speaking to the—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Oh, we will hear from the Hon Steven Joyce.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: As I recall the question in this particular instance, it asked
about a piece of information a nd then went on to ask some other things, so the question
then becomes whether the Minister is ent itled to make a response to the broader
elements of the question if he or she does not have that particular detail in front of him
or her. I think that to suggest that is not  possible is perhaps making it quite hard for
Ministers to determine how exactly to respond to a question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I appreciate—[ Interruption] I do not need to hear any more. I
appreciate the comments that have come from  both sides of the House. With regard to
Grant Robertson’s point, the previous Sp eaker did establish a very good habit of
ensuring that where a clear question is aske d, it deserves a concise and clear answer. If
that answer is that the Minister doesn’t ha ve the facts, I still think that on occasions
there will be the opportunity, and there shoul d be the opportunity, for the Minister to
explain why he might not have those facts. So I accept the points that have been raised
by all members, particularly Grant Roberts on, and I will endeavour to see that we get
sharp answers to sharp questions.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If it is a fresh point of order, I will hear it for certain.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Yes, it is. I thank you for your ruling. The only other point I
would raise—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is a point of order and it will be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: —and on which I would seek your guidance—because I
think you may have inadverten tly made reference to the exchange between the Minister
and me yesterday, and that is fair enough. Bu t you have ruled, and I think it was quite a
new ruling, and you have ruled on a number of occasions over  subsequent months, that
if a member gets a direct yes or no answer , or whatever, and is satisfied with that
ruling—and you have stuck up for our right to do so—we can rise and say we are
satisfied with that and move on. You did that with me yesterday, for instance, here.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is exactly the point I am rais ing, so it is hardly a fresh point of
order. I am saying to the member, partic ularly in light of my reviewing the Hansard
yesterday, that if he takes the opportunity of doing that, it is not strictly a point of order,
and the risk for any member who does that wi ll be for me to immediately move to the
next question.
11270 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Jun 2013

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Then is it correct that, accord ing to the Reserve Bank, the level
of borrowing for residentia l housing has increased by arou nd $10 billion over the past
year; if so, how much additional debt does he  expect New Zealanders will take on to
buy houses over the next year, with house pri ce inflation in Auckland currently running
at 15 percent?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Again, I can say that I do not have those specific numbers
in front of me, in light of the primary question, but the point that I can—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Which was about debt—excessive debt.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, it was actually about—yes, but not about elements of
it. But the point I would make is that in term s of the increase in residential debt that is
coming off a period post - global financial crisis that was significantly lower, but,
nevertheless, the Government is concerned ab out increasing levels of residential debt,
which is why we are very, very focused on making sure that we increase the supply of
houses in Auckland to ensure that there ar e opportunities for people to purchase houses
at lower levels of debt than they have been able to do in the past.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I seek leave to table the Reserve Bank data series to show that
the debt figures and increases are as I have said.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It is available to all members, I think, is it not?

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Point of order, Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Perhaps if the member could tell us the source of the document.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: It is Table C6 from the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, but—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Which is available, I pr esume, on their website. [ Interruption] No.
Order!
Skycity, Convention Centre—Transparency of Process
3. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statement that “In 2009, New Z ealand was rated first on the Transparency
International’s ‘Corruption Perception Index’. Out of 180 countries, New Zealand was
rated as having the lowest pe rceived public sector corruptio n. As a nation, that ranking
is something of which we can be very proud”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, and I note that the 2010, 2011, and
2012 indexes all show New Zealand maintaining its  position as first or first equal in the
rankings.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is he concerned that Transp arency International, whose
Corruption Perceptions Index he  rightly holds in such high  regard, has highlighted his
own convention-centre-for-pokies deal as raising concerns from both a fiscal
transparency, accountability, and a regulatory perspective; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, and the reason for that is that this deal will be in full view
for the public. We campaigned on the issue pr ior to the election. The agreement will be
in the public domain when it is fully signed by both parties. The legislation supporting it
will go through a select committee process, and the Auditor-General had a thorough
look at the process and, for the most part, was happy.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: So is the Prime Minister saying that Transparency International
is wrong?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, and the Government has b een very transparent about its
dealings with Skycity. Unlike some political parties, we do not do our negotiations in a
box on a Saturday night at the All Blacks game. We do it—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The question has been answered. [Interruption] Order!

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he agree—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The level of interjections coming now from both sides of the
House is unacceptable for Dr Norman to ask his supplementary question.
26 Jun 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 11271

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he agree with Transparen cy International that the public
procurement process in the Skycity project was severely compromised?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, and neither does the Auditor-General.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he disagree, then, with the Auditor-General, when she
found that the evaluation process for the c onvention centre bids was neither transparent
nor even-handed?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not agree with the Auditor-General on that basic point. I
think it is worth remembering, if we go through the process one more time, that this is a
deal that we campaigned on, this is a deal where the full agreement of all the terms and
conditions will be in the public domain for ever ybody to see, this is a deal that will be
supported by legislation that will go through a full select committee process, and this is
a deal where the Auditor-General actually found, broadly speaking, she was happy. The
point that the Auditor-General did not like was the point that we have traversed in this
House many times before. She believed that  the officials shoul d have stopped the
process at a point where it was clear that Skycity was the likely preferred candidate, and
in fact the Government’s view was we needed to get more information.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is it then the Prime Minister’s position that Transparency
International is wrong when it said the Skycity project procurement process was
severely compromised, and is it his position that the Auditor-General is wrong when the
Auditor-General found that th e evaluation process was neit her transparent nor even-
handed—the Prime Minister is  always right; and Transpar ency International and the
Auditor-General, they are just wrong?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I could not put it better myself. Yes, they are wrong.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he intend to ignore all of  the different legal and academic
voices, such as the Law Society, Transparency  International, and the Auditor-General,
who have all raised concerns about the way th is Government treats the rule of law and
the proper procurement process, and is he concerned that he will corrode the good
reputation that the New Zealand Government had when he came into office?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The Government is always going  to be active across a wide
range of fronts. We are a busy Government and there will always be people who offer
views, and sometimes we will not agree with them. But I point out to the member again
that New Zealand ranked No. 1 in its own right or first equal in the years 2010, 2011,
and 2012. They happen to be all the years I was Prime Minister of  New Zealand. I am
not the one who sneaks off to Skycity’s box and has a little—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The question has been adequately addressed.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I wish to raise the issue that
you yourself spoke of previously.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is a point of order, and it will be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: The point that we have been re ferring to is Standing Order 383,
“Content of replies”, which states: “The re ply to any question must be concise and
confined to the subject-matter of the question asked,”. The Prime Minister repeatedly,
during the course of these questions, breached  that Standing Order. I would ask you
what is your remedy to deal w ith the fact that the Prime Mi nister consistently breaches
Standing Order 383?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member asked me questi ons about transparency and
openness in relation to Skycity. I made the Government’s position very clear. I also
contrasted it with the beha viour I saw from other politi cal parties. That is quite
legitimate public answering.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Supplementary question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I have just got to rule on a point of order that has been raised by
Dr Russel Norman. I ask Dr Russel Norman to  have a close look at  the content of his
11272 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Jun 2013
question in line with Standing Order 377. If he  can get his questions concise, he can
expect a concise answer.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Did Skycity donate money to the National Party in 2011; if
so, how much?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I have no responsibility for that.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I did not ask the Prime
Minister about his responsib ilities. I asked him a simple question: how much did
Skycity give you in 2011?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Well, Skycity certainly di d not give me anything, but the
Prime Minister stood up and sa id he does not have any re sponsibility. That was his
answer to the question.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. It is a well-established
tradition that if in the answers that the Pr ime Minister gives he introduces subject

planned for the impact of this event and were able to maintain essential services while
responding to calls for assistance. Emergency services, civil defence staff, and council
crews have all worked extremely hard in difficult and dangerous conditions, sometimes
with real risks to themselves. I want to acknowledge them and thank them for their
service.

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: What lessons does the Minister believe can be taken away from
this most recent storm?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: As with all scenarios involving extreme weather, people should
pay close attention to advice from local authorities and civil defence emergency
management groups. It is also important for people to reach out to neighbours and
people in communities who may be vulnerable during these times. The recent response
to extreme weather has demonstrated the effectiveness of community-based civil
defence organisations and reinforces that our  civil defence structure is working well.
Local knowledge is vital for effectively re sponding to local ev ents. I would again
commend the emergency services, civil defenc e staff, and council crews who have all
worked so hard over the last week to minimise the impact of the storm.
Prostitution Reform Act 2003—Bylaw-making Powers and Potential Legislative
Changes
12. Le’aufa’amulia ASENAT I LOLE-TAYLOR (NZ First)  to the Prime

items.speaker: Minister
items.text: Does he still stand by his reported statement that the Prostitution Law Reform
Act 2003 “hasn’t actually worked”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes. One of the key purposes of the
Prostitution Reform Act was to prohibit pr ostitution for under-18-year-olds. I do not
believe it has been effective in doing that.
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor : What progress, if any, has his Government
made in addressing street prostitution since he stated in December of last year in regard
to street prostitution that “the Government is looking to, through the Local Government
Act, make other changes that would support local government.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, I think that the member—because she has an interest in
this issue, and I accept that—is aware that the matter is before the select committee. I
think also that the Government’s view has been consistent in this matter, and it is that
the Local Government Act, on the advice that we have had, does empower the territorial
authorities to make by-laws for the issues that have been mentioned. The Government’s
view, therefore, is that no t only do the councils have the capacity to do that through the
26 Jun 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 11281
Local Government Act, but also if there was to be a change to gi ve the local councils
even greater powers, then I think the Govern ment’s view would be that that should be
spread across all councils around New Zealand, not something specific to Manukau.
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor : Given that answer, does he then agree with
his National Party colleagues that in regard to the issue of street prostitution
“Government has continued to pass responsibi lity to local councils and as a result is
causing ratepayer costs and consequential rate increases.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Firstly, I think it would be us eful if the member were to
reference that quote to the member who made it, because otherwise I cannot be sure of
its authenticity. But what I can say is that  it has been a longstanding practice that in
these areas the matters are handled, and righ tfully so, by local government. That is why
the Local Government Act actually empowers  councils to make by-laws to prohibit
street prostitution.
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor: Given that sad response—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Would the member please ask the supplementary question.
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor : I am getting there. Is the Prime Minister
aware of a legal opinion made available to the Auckland Council that advises that
enforceable by-laws cannot be made to re strict trading hours or  areas for street
prostitution because any such by-law will bo th contravene the Prostitution Reform Act
and potentially run foul of othe r Acts of Government, and wh at does he have to say to
residents and ratepayers of Hunters Co rner, Papatoetoe, and numerous other
communities in South Auckland and across the country who have to deal day after day
with the numerous health and safety issues that street prostitution causes in their
communities?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, I have not seen that lega l opinion. I am aware of Crown
Law’s view, which is that the Local Govern ment Act does support territorial authorities
to make by-laws. In fact, I would point out  to the member that the Auckland Council,
when it put out its report in May 2012 called The street prostitution industry in the
southern communities of Auckland , at page 12 actually set out quite clearly how the
Local Government Act does support authori ties in terms of making those by-laws. I
think the point the member is making is that maybe those by-laws need to be widened.
That may or may not be a fair point. The poi nt I would simply make to the member is
that if that law were to be progressed further, in my view, it should be expanded beyond
just the streets of Manukau, and if that were the case, we may well look at it.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: I move, That the House
take note of miscellaneous business. I woke up at 5.30 this morning and, as is my wont,
the first thing I did was lunge for my BlackBerry so I could read the New Zealand
Herald. The first thing I saw was the Herald-DigiPoll, and I thought to myself: “I like
history, especially the hist ory of the Labour Party. I w onder whether Gerry would let
me give one of my history lessons to the Hous e.” I asked him, and he said yes, so here
goes.
One of the great questions of New Zealand history is: “Why is th e Labour Party so
disloyal to its leaders?”. Ri ght through history, treachery has been the name of the
game. Let us look at Arnold Nordmeyer, w ho provided sterling service to the Labour
Party through the first and second Labour  Governments. He was the MP for Ōāmaru,
then the MP for Brooklyn, and then the MP for Island Bay. He was knifed by Norman
Kirk. The rumblings against “Big Norm” started in the second year of his premiership,
but he died before the conspirators could knife him.
11282 General Debate 26 Jun 2013
Then there was my favourite Labour leader, Bill Rowli ng, a good and a decent man
who, as Mr Mallard knows, used to liv e in Lohia Street, Khandallah. He was
undermined by a less talented but more ruth less deputy. How often history doth repeat
itself. David Lange was undermined by Mr Goff and his then ideological buddy Roger
Douglas. Geoffrey Palmer was certainly an interesting person. He certainly was
undermined by Helen Clark and by Mike Moore, but I have to admit that much of the
undermining was done by Geoffrey just being Geoffrey.
Mike Moore was undermined by Helen Clark, who knifed him straight after the 1993
election, when Mike had gained an additional 16 seats for his party—that is loyalty for
you. Helen Clark knew her histor y. She kept her enemies at bay, and I am not referring
to just the Green Party. She saw off A nnette King and Phil Goff in 1996, when they
tried to knife her, and she went in 2008, befo re the daggers went in. Then from 2008 to
2011 we had that very angry Phil Goff, undermined from the very start by Mr
Cunliffe—no wonder he is so foul-mouthed and cannot control his tongue.
I recognise that many of the names I ha ve referred to—and I see Mr Robertson
looking confused and bewildered—will be unk nown to people like Mr Robertson, who
have no knowledge of their party’s history, and so are doomed to relive it. It is like
some kind of macabre Byzantine dance of kill ers. People cooperate to get rid of one
leader, so that they can turn on the next one.
Then we have David Shearer, who, I think, is a very nice guy, a good and a decent
man, a person who has done a lot of good ov erseas. But none of his dealings with
central African dictatorships or Balkan ci vil wars could have prepared him for the
leadership of the Labour Party. Poor David Shearer. He has run out of options. He has
nowhere to turn. He cannot rely  on his deputy and he cannot tu rn to his allies. I bet this
morning he was reading the New Zealand Herald , looking longingly at seat 17A from
Moscow to Havana.
Mr Shearer has been quoted as saying th at he was surprised by today’s results, but
the trouble for Mr Shearer is he is simply too trusting. He is too trusting and too quick
to trust people like Mr Robertson to recruit his staff to look after him. He is too quick to
trust parties that are out to steal his vote. I imagine that Mr Shearer was delighted when
Mr Peters shone that trademar k smile and offered to work with Labour to attack the
Government. I imagine he was delighted when Dr Russel Norman said: “Let me work
with you to design a Stalinist energy policy, and maybe it w ould be a good idea if we
both had a podium in the legislative chamber when we announce the speech, because it
would give you more gravitas.” And now Mr Shearer is surprised that Mr Peters and Mr
Norman are laughing all the way to the polling  booth. In fact, he is so trusting that I
have to say I really worry that the hundreds of thousands of dollars in his New York
bank account are ripe for picking if a Nigerian scammer ever sends him an email. He
would probably be really surpri sed and delighted to receive it. So what is the moral of
the story? There is always a moral. I say th is to the Labour Party, with the greatest of
respect and affection: loyalty is what binds  a party together. If you can’t trust your
leader, you’re done.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: Well, that was a very entertaining history
lesson from Chris Finlayson, but he had nothing to say about the Government’s policies,
and that is not surprising, because they get all of their best ones from the Labour Party.
Despite the hilarity from Mr Finlayson, these Government members are kidding
themselves that they can govern on their own after 2014. They are desperately casting
around for coalition partners. They do not have one—the mad, the bad, and the sad are
on the way out. There are no coalition part ners left. They are desperately casting
around, and what better thing to do than to st eal one of the Labour Party’s most popular
policies. Mr Brownlee—yes, I am talking about you.
26 Jun 2013 General Debate 11283
This is the background to what today is one  of the most stunning policy U-turns that
we have seen for a very long time. John Key is the first Prime Mini ster ever to do a U-
turn in a train. It is the first time it has been done. This is a huge about-face. Mr
Brownlee only days ago was describing the Ci ty Rail Link, the polic y that he supports
today, as a short, little loop. I wondered, in fact, whethe r he was talking about Mr
Finlayson, but, no, he was talking about the City Rail Link. He also said that he doubted
whether the City Rail Link was, indeed, either popular or useful. That flew in the face of
popular opinion in Auckland. We know that 63 percent of Aucklanders in the last
independent poll—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Agreed with Labour.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: —agreed with Labour that the City Rail Link was a no-brainer.
Well, Labour welcomes this U-turn—we do. We welcome it. It was our policy. The
Government has adopted it. That is great. It is a win for Len Brown, it is a win for
Labour, and it is a win for Auckland.
Unlike the Government’s flagship policy projects—the so-called “motorways of
madness”—the City Rail Link will actually double the capacity of an existing transport
asset. The Minister of Transport’s motorw ay projects are all gold-plated duplicate
projects, and he is spending $1 billion every year on them. Well, the City Rail Link will
double the capacity of the Auckland rail netw ork. It will allow trains to run every 5
minutes—every 5 minutes—on the western and southern lines. If you are travelling
from New Lynn to the central business distri ct, into the city, it will cut 28 minutes—28
minutes—off your commute. That is three times  as much time cut off travel as that
member’s Pūhoi to Wellsford “Holiday Highway” would do.
So what this U-turn says is that the credibility of the Government’s transport policy
is in tatters. What are we supposed to beli eve? Was Steven Joyce wrong when he said
only a few weeks ago that the City Rail Link did not add up? Was Gerry Brownlee
serious when he compared the City Rail Li nk to the failed North Haverbrook monorail
in The Simpsons? And for what new transport polic ies will Gerry Brownlee be getting
inspiration from The Simpsons ? What new thing will we see? I hope the Minister is
going to take a call and tell us.
What has changed, Minister? The numbers ha ve not changed. The plan for the City
Rail Link has not changed. The number of Aucklanders who support this project has not
changed. What has changed? You see, the bi g losers today are Steven Joyce and Gerry
Brownlee. They have been made to look lik e total idiots by their own Government, but,
as I said, Labour welcomes this U-turn. I think the question we have to ask is: “Why did
it take so long, Gerry?”. Why did it take so l ong? I am going to answer that question for
you because there are two reasons that it has taken so long. The first is that National
members have a completely messed up, tortur ed relationship with Auckland. Anything
that Len Brown supports, these guys oppos e—no matter how sensible, no matter how
popular—because their man, John Banks, did no t win the Auckland ma yoralty in 2010.
They have never got over it, and they have sp ent the last 5 years bagging the City Rail
Link and leading Aucklanders on a wild goose chase that has finally ended today with
the Government adopting one of Labour’s most popular policies.
The other point I want to make is that the City Rail Link symbolises the urban,
modern vision that Labour has for Auckland. Steven Joyce, Gerry Brownlee, and Nick
Smith simply do not understand it. They do not get it. They are out of step with
Auckland, and that is why it ha s taken them 5 years to adopt  what is an incredibly
popular policy. This is a win for Labour, it is  a win for Mayor Len Brown, and it is a
win for Auckland.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I think it is no surprise that
Phil Twyford comes into the House this afternoon and mounts a sterling case for the job
11284 General Debate 26 Jun 2013
of stationmaster at Britomart after the next election. Anybody who saw the front page of
the New Zealand Herald this morning will know that five  members sitting on that side
of the House are gone at the next election. The question has to be asked about why the
Opposition is so bad. Why is it not getting traction with the New Zealand public? David
Shearer comes out this morning and says th at Opposition members have spent the last 5
weeks talking about the things that New Zealanders want to  talk about. That would be
the opposition to the casino, the Government Communications Security Bureau matters,
the Peter Dunne issues, the increased taxes on the properties that New Zealanders might
own, and then the Opposition’s manufacturing inquiry, which basically concluded that
if you took out all of the grow ing parts of the manufacturi ng sector, the rest of it was
failing. It is that sort of misconnection with the people of New Zealand that is leading to
the result that we saw in the New Zealand Herald poll this morning. No one gets too
excited about that on this side of the House. Our pledge is to cont inue with the job of
governing and getting on with making sure th at the growth engine of the New Zealand
economy is fuelled by our policies.
The Labour Party members may well want to gloat that somehow our decision to put
a time line and some conditions around our support for the rail link in Auckland is a win
for them. The reality is that we have always  maintained that we would be looking at a
wholly integrated transport network for New Zealand’s largest and fastest-growing city.
New Zealand is littered with examples of ho w there has been a failure to futureproof,
and so we think that 2020 for that loop a nd the construction of the extension of
Britomart would be the right thing to do. Th at will come with some conditions, which
will be announced by the Prime Minister on Friday.
But also we have the extensive roll-out  of broadband across New Zealand. We are
seeing all sorts of innovations in our economy taking advantage of that and anticipating
the advantage that will come from that. We  are also seeing across the legislative
programme the Business Growth Agenda simp lifying the activity of doing business in
New Zealand, meaning that there is a greater opportunity for job creation and for higher
wages and salaries for New Zealanders. We have seen the Hon Chris Finlayson engaged
in one of the most rapid settlements of Tr eaty issues ever undertaken by any Minister,
and that is good for a large section of our  population and we fully support it. We are
also very committed to the rebuild in Christchurch.
Those are the things that New Zealanders do talk about. They are the things that they
look to a Government to be doing. They are the things that they look  at and expect the
Government to be providing. We have another big announcement tomorrow around
Christchurch, where we are talking about th e conclusion of the co st-sharing agreement
between the Christchurch City Council and the Govern ment. That will mark a
significant point for stepping up the rebuild of  that city. I look forward to joining the
Prime Minister when those announcements are made at about midday tomorrow.
On Friday the Prime Minister will addre ss a number of issues that are in the
Auckland Plan, and will outline the Government’s response to those things. Transport is
part of that, and the rail loop is just a small part of that. There are going to be some very
interesting announcements made in that speech, which will be  well received by
Aucklanders, that demonstrate this Gove rnment’s commitment to New Zealand’s
biggest city, a day after we have made a big commitment to Ne w Zealand’s second-
biggest city.
Throughout the country there are transport programmes that will oil the wheels of
economic growth. Then, if you look at social services, the work that is going on in the
education sector, the extraordinary work of  Tony Ryall in the health sector, and so
many other areas where the Government is simp ly getting on with the job, it is not hard
to understand why New Zealanders are not connecting with a party that is focused
26 Jun 2013 General Debate 11285
entirely on the office boy issues of the beltway, the Government Communications
Security Bureau, Mr Dunne, the so-called inquiry into manufacturing, and opposition to
everything that is about growth. My final comment for Mr Twyford is that I thought he,
of all people, would by now have realised that every loop has a U-turn in it.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Kia
ora tātou e te Whare. I do not intend to try to  even follow up on the speech given by the
Hon Chris Finlayson, but I do want to address, in the 5 minutes I have, an issue that has
come that is a little bit more human. I want to do it by way of a story. It comes from my
electorate, and it is fairly recent.
At the dawn of 15 October 2007, in a Whakat āne home, a man and a woman and a
17-year-old girl were asleep in bed, blissfully unaware that at 6 a.m. sharp that morning,
14 officers of the Special Tactics Group and the armed offenders squad would cordon
off the address, shouting for the occupants to  leave the address with their hands on their
heads. The man was arrested, forced to lie on the floor, and was handcuffed. The two
women were separated from each other a nd searched. The older woman was in a
nightgown and the younger woman in a thin si nglet and shorts. She remembered later
feeling ashamed and embarrassed, and burstin g out crying. After being detained, the
two women were taken to the police station, separated again, and statements were
obtained. They were still in their nightw ear. They were cold. The older woman, who
was a diabetic, required her insulin and her testing kit.
Nearly 6 years after that event, Judge Carruthers, the Chair of the Independent Police
Conduct Authority, wrote to them, and I want to  just draw the attention of the House to
the letter, where it refers to the impact of  fear and anxiety experienced by those three
people. The judge said this: “being woke n in the early morning by armed offenders
shouting for them to come out of their hous e with their hands on their heads, having
guns trained on them, a dog barking throughout,  being barefoot and only dressed in
nightwear, and scared about what was happeni ng to them ... these actions ... personally
searching them in an  intrusive manner, and taking th em to the police station, were
contrary to law.” The letter concludes that “T he arbitrary detention was contrary to law,
unjustified, and unreasonable.”
If these words sound pretty familiar, it is because these same words were repeated
consistently throughout the re port of the Independent Po lice Conduct Authority into
Operation Eight. The key thing here is th at over a month has passed, has gone by us,
since the police were said to have acted unlawfully in establis hing roadblocks and
detaining and searching people during Operation Eight. But what has happened to those
people affected? What has happened to thos e who were traumatised and suffered the
consequences of the unlawful actions by our  key agents of the law? Nothing—nothing.
No acknowledgment to the people who were hurt. No apology. No attempt to meet
kanohi ki te kanohi, face to face, or even to ask any question. What now? Nothing. I
bring that story to this House.
We came here as a M āori Party to protect the interests of M āori people and advance
our potential into the future. We came here  on the back of the Labour Government’s
decision to confiscate the foreshore and seabed area of our country. So when this second
invasion of rights occurr ed in the raids upon the T ūhoe people and the wh ānau of the
Rūatoki Valley, the M āori Party has again challenge d the Government, the Labour
Government, about its unlawful practice. Indeed it is a cont empt for the very notion of
due process under law.
I want to tell this House and the New Zeal and public that this issue, the unlawful
treatment of a family in Whakat āne and the many other familie s who were subjected to
the abuses meted out under the name of Operation Eight, will not be left to linger. It will
not be left to linger. The M āori Party and I as the MP are determined to ensure that
11286 General Debate 26 Jun 2013
those whānau who were affected know th at they are not alone. So  I want to advise this
House that the M āori Party will be taking this up with  some vigour. As recently as this
morning I placed a tono in front of the Māori Affairs Committee to tell it that we will be
presenting terms of reference for an inquiry  about the impact of Operation Eight on
affected people, and that will come in front of this House at some point in time in the
future. Tēnā koutou. Kia ora tātou.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: Today is a fantastic
day for the Labour Party, and it is a very, ve ry bad day—it is a very, very bad day—for
Gerry Brownlee and a very, very bad day for Steven Joyce. Poor Gerry Brownlee during
question time had to stand th ere and take the questions from Phil Twyford, and Gerry
Brownlee—you could see it in his face. He wanted the Earth to open up and swallow
him whole, but, unfortunately for Gerry, even the planet doe s not have that kind of
appetite. Even the planet could not swallo w Gerry Brownlee whol e. He had to stand
there and take it today as he realised th at his Government had done another U-turn,
another backflip, which has become the trademark of this National Government.
Sitting next to him was Steven Joyce. I have never seen Steven Joyce squirm as
much as he did during question time today. Normally he looks like he is plotting.
Normally he looks like he is scheming—the  Machiavellian machine of the National
Party, trying to figure out how he is going to see off Judith Collins after the next
election when John Key has to stand down—b ut he did not look happy today. He was
not plotting and scheming today. He was sq uirming because National has been found
out. It has finally had to si gn up to the Auckland City Ra il Link, which is so popular
with Aucklanders.
It makes economic sense, and it is somethi ng that the Labour Party has been calling
for for years. It was in our election manifesto at the last election. That is how committed
the Labour Party has been to the Auckland City Rail Link. That is how committed we
are to sensible investment in transport infrastructure for Auckland.
Steven Joyce and Gerry Brownl ee would like you to think that  this is just a slight
change—that this is just a time frame that they are adding to their lukewarm
commitment to the Auckland City Rail Link. But this is what Steven Joyce had to say
about it. When Steven Joyce was asked whether there was anybody who was less
enthusiastic about the Auckland City Rail  Link, he said: “Hmm, well, possibly the
finance Minister.” Steven Joyce was happy and proud to say that he was the person who
was least enthusiastic about the Auckland C ity Rail Link. That is what he thought about
it. Gerry Brownlee said that he thought that it was neither useful nor popular.
National’s position on rail has been absolutely clear for years, but National members,
of course, like typical conservatives, are al ways the last ones to  the party. They are
always the last ones to figure out what is th e right thing to do. La bour has been talking
about this for years, Mayor Len Brown has been talking about this for years, and Mayor
Len Brown has got a consensus around this issue: the business groups, the community
groups, the unions—everybody in Auckland want s this. The only people who did not
want it were in the National Government. They  have finally decided that they have to
come round. They do not agree with it, they do not like it, but they realise that they are
wrong and we are right, and it is as simple as that.
But, of course, National does not believe in  rail and it is still allowing its obsession
with the roads of national significance to  dictate all investment in transport
infrastructure.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: They’re delaying the rail tunnel.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: It is delaying the rail link and it is delaying anything to
do with rail, so when will this be built? We ll, it might get started in 2020, if we are
lucky. Why is that? Because there is nothing left. The cupboard is bare. All the money
26 Jun 2013 General Debate 11287
has been spent on unecono mic, monster motorways up and down the country. The
Pūhoi to Wellsford “Holiday Highway” is still more important to the National
Government than the Auckland City Rail Link. That is why it cannot afford to build it
now. That is why Aucklanders have to wait until 2020. Roads and highways are still the
trump card in the National Government’s transport policy.
National does not believe in having a sensib le transport strategy. It does not believe
in having an integrated transport system. It believes only in having highways. That is all
that it believes in. There is no sense to it. It is just th e National Government’s fixation,
and, of course, it is the fixation with roads of the supporters of National, the people who
fund the National Party. It is their fixation with roads that  is dominating the National
Government’s policy. That is why that Government over there will never invest in an
integrated transport network, and that is why it has been so sl ow to catch up with
everybody else who has been calling for the Auckland City Rail Link for years.
Thank goodness National has finally seen  sense and it has finally decided to
implement a wonderful Labour policy. It is a great day for Labour. We look forward to
National implementing more and more Labour policy, because it is the only place that
the good ideas come from.

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: It is not surprising that the
public often have a low opinion of politicians, especially if they ha ve been listening to
the Opposition speakers this afternoon, because  they so often focus on the small, the
niggly, the irrelevant, the unim portant, and even the self-s erving. But people vote for a
Government that focuses on the things that  matter to them. Things that focus on the
safety of the nation: security in their homes; better, sooner, more convenient healthcare;
quality education for their kids; and a pub lic safety net for when things go pear-
shaped—pear-shaped for individuals, pear -shaped for communities. Certainly the
people of Canterbury are appreciative of this Government standing up and backing them
emotionally and financially as we manage our way through the recovery. John Key and
the National-led Government are absolutely committed to getting right the things that
matter most to Kiwis, and in the face of  an ongoing international meltdown we are
making good progress. Our economy is growing faster than that of most countries. We
have a lower unemployment rate than mo st countries. And our mortgage rates,
something that affects every single New Zealander, are the lowest for over 45 years.
And that is the problem for Opposition politicians. That is why we hear only tired old
rhetoric—because they cannot talk about the things that matter, because those are good-
news stories. They have to focus on the sm all, the niggly, and the irrelevant, or you
could conjure up a false crisis like the manu facturing crisis. They spent months talking
up the manufacturing crisis, months dumpi ng on manufacturers, who are actually
working very hard to manage and produce in very difficult times. Luckily, they
announced their crisis findings about the same time as independent data confirmed that
New Zealand manufacturing was growing at the fastest rate since 2004 and one of the
highest rates across the worl d. I say “luckily” because no w the public know the facts
and can decide for themselves.
Opposition politicians talk the talk of activity, of positivity. They say they want more
jobs, they say they want better incomes, but they do not walk the walk. They say no to
everything that might help create jobs or lift incomes, and they talk of embracing
change and innovation but vote against anythi ng that would improve our chances of a
better future. And they do it so consistently that I fear they are deliberately undermining
the well-being of Kiwis simply because they cannot stand the fact and the reality that
New Zealanders are doing well under this National Government.
Well, our Government, the National G overnment, celebrates success. We are
working hard to deliver real jobs, real grow th, and real progress for Kiwi families. We
11288 General Debate 26 Jun 2013
are delighted that after-tax wages have in creased by 22 percent since 2008 and that the
cost of living rises are the lowest since 1999, and we will be continuing to work hard to
improve these statistics. We thank the po lice and community organisations for the
lowest crime rate for 30 years and we thank everyone in health who has worked so hard
to deliver more elective operations and faster  emergency treatment so that every cancer
patient can be treated right here in New Zeal and in the world gold standard of 4 weeks.
Finally, we congratulate the education sect or on continuing to deliver world-class
education for our young people. We know that , but it has just be en confirmed by the
OECD’s latest report—well done.
So, in conclusion, in the toughest of time s, New Zealand and New Zealanders are
working hard and doing well, and that is something to celebrate. So I say to the

items.speaker: Opposition
items.text: try to do something that matters for our country. Do not knock New

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: It is a bleak time in the histor y of this country, a time when
our constitution and the rule of law are being flippantl y—albeit sometimes elegantly—
undermined. We are being spun the lie that it is for our own good, that there was no
other choice, that the people who are dissenting on this issue are just wrong, and that the
Government is always right. Yet the rule of  law, human rights, and our constitution are
fundamental to our society. They guarantee th at everyone should get their day in court,
that people should be equal be fore the law, that the cour ts and the Government should
be blind to the size of our wallets and to any of our many other differences, and that
there should be an even playing field on which that contest of ideas should take place.
As a country we have long signed up to th ese understandings. These agreements are
at the very foundation of our democracy, and I think that most New Zealanders are very
proud of that and understand th at we are lucky to have th at at the foundation of our
country. In a speech earlier this month, though, Russel Norman signalled that something
seemed a bit rotten in the Beehive, and he noted: “Our democracy is being eaten away
by a Government that persistently underm ines our basic democratic rights and
institutions …”. There was a strong reaction to that speec h and a lot of disagreement,
yet his view was vindicated last week, I believe, by the New Zealand Law Society.
Last week the New Zealand Law Society, a bo dy created by statute with the role of
providing submissions on legislation on behalf of the law fraternity, reported to the UN
periodic review of human right s that 14 separate pi eces of legislati on, 11 in the last 2
years, have undermined the rule of law a nd our fundamental human rights. Of these,
five laws remove the court’s constitutional role of judicial review, three laws give
unjustifiable power to the executive, five la ws breach the New Zealand Bill of Rights
Act, four laws were passed amidst very  serious human rights concerns, and this
Government and this House are currently c onsidering another thre e bills with further
serious human rights concerns. Six of these bills removed rights from New Zealanders
in what I would kind of characterise as an effort to appeal to the “get tough on crime’
crowd in New Zealand—in the face of all the evidence that that approach does not
work. It seems symbolic of this Government ’s view that, actuall y, we cannot do things
to create safety in our society without removing somebody’s fundamental rights and the
role of the courts.
The Government has also introduced two laws  to this House in a similar vein—the
Government Communications Security Bur eau and Related Legislation Amendment
Bill and the Telecommunications (Intercepti on Capability and Security) Bill, which
remove rights while increasi ng surveillance—all unde r the sense of creating threat, the
idea that we need to be protecting New Zealanders from some unnamed and
unsubstantiated danger that this Government will not disclose. Other bills have removed
26 Jun 2013 General Debate 11289
democracy from Christchurch, and removed environmental protections as well as
democracy from the wider Canterbury area.
The Government has entrenched discrimi nation against women on the DPB. It has
removed the rights of judicial review, and it has entrenched discrimination against some
of the most vulnerable people in New Zealand —people with disabilities who want to be
cared for by family members. It has rem oved rights and entrenched discrimination
against some of the world’s most vulnerabl e people—asylum seekers who need to seek
asylum in this country.
Also, there are numerous examples of the Government favouring its mates. It has
introduced what we call the Anadarko law to make protests on the sea illegal. It has
been indulging in dodgy Skycity deals. What it is all about, when it comes down to it, is
a misuse of power, and this country deserves more.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call
in the general debate this afternoon. It is a pleasure because in this House we debate
social, economic, and political issues of  the day. Whether we are talking about
partnership schools or we  are talking about the social se rvices that are delivered across
this nation or we are talking about the busin esses that provide jobs and opportunities for
New Zealanders, the one common denominato r is leadership. When I read this
morning’s latest Herald-DigiPoll party vote figures, they clearly show where the
leadership is found in this country—48.8 percent support National on a party vote basis,
and Labour is down five and a half points to 30.9 percent. It is about leadership.
Mr Key is the most preferred Prime Mini ster at 65 percen t—65 percent of New
Zealanders want the John Key - led Government to continue the fine work that we have
been doing as a Government in the last 4½ ye ars. It is 12 percent for Mr Shearer. Has
someone told Grant Robertson about Mr Shearer being at 12 percent? We have even got
Miss Clark from New York at 3 percent. Can you believe it? Ca n you believe it? A
former leader of the Labour Party is at 3 pe rcent. But what this poll shows is that New
Zealanders fundamentally do not want what  Labour is selling. They do not want the
profanity-laced mutterings in select comm ittees from old MPs like Mr Goff and Mr
Mallard, they do not want the fondue dinners  in Wellington Central that are going to
lead to a leadership spill in the coming months, and they do not  want the backroom
deals of the faceless men in our union offices  across this country determining the future
of this country. So, Labour, take heed. Take  heed of the Rudd-Gill ard dispute, because
it is coming to New Zealand in the form of Robertson versus  Cunliffe—Robertson
versus Cunliffe—and you heard it right here.
But the good thing is that New Zealanders want leadership and they want vision. The
reason why National is polling 48.8 percent is that New Zealanders know that this party
focuses on the issues that matter to them. They know that National cares about all New
Zealanders. The last Budget is a demonstration of that carin g, and of that efficient way
that National goes about bringi ng about the issues that matter to New Zealanders. What
are those issues? Well, we know  that 50,000 jobs have been cr eated in the last 2 years.
When I go across my electorate in Maungakiekie , when I go and talk to the constituents
with whom I had clinics last week, and when I talk to the businesses, they say that the
No. 1 priority of this Government should be  creating jobs, and th at is what we are
doing.
Household incomes are up 20 percent since 2008. Household incomes are up—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Median incomes are down.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: —and the mortgage rates, Mr Clark, are at their lowest
in 50 years. Mortgage interest rates are at  their lowest in 50 years. They reached 8
percent under the Clark Government—not  David Clark but the Helen Clark
Government—and they were at their highest peak for a very, very long time.
11290 General Debate 26 Jun 2013
When I held those clinics in Mount Wellington and Onehunga last week, what
constituents said to me is that they want jobs but they also want  safety, so they are
really happy that there are more front-line policemen across this nation than there ever
have been in our history. They wanted health  care that was caring, but they also wanted
health care that looked after their elderly and looked after their kids. There are 1,000
extra doctors and 2,500 extra nurses working today than there were under the Labour
Government in 2008. [Interruption] We know—and Mr Mallard knows this—that there
are more patients getting elective operations  and seeing specia lists sooner in our
hospitals today than there ever were under the Labour Government.
I went to the Tāmaki opening last week, and this was symbolic of what is going on in
this country. One hundred pe ople were inside Ruap ōtaka Marae celebrating what
National is bringing to my local community in T āmaki. What were they celebrating?
They were celebrating warmer, drier homes. Wh at were they celebr ating? They were
celebrating ultra-fast broadba nd coming to their schools. Wh at were they celebrating?
They were celebrating the Auckland-Manuka u Eastern Transport Initiative, which
brings transport links into a nd around Auckland in order to speed up travel, not just for
residents but for businesses as well.
This is a Government that is doing things, progressing this country, and delivering on
the promises that we made in the 2011 election. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I have to ask the question: why is
that member not in Cabinet? Why is Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga not a member of the Cabinet,
when it put in other members who do not have  the gravitas and the intellect of the
member who has just spoken? No wonder he is an unhappy member of that caucus. He
is looking at a party that saw a drop of 6 percent in one poll very recently, and he knows
that it has a party leader who has lost 30 percentage points in his own popularity in 1
year alone, and that the track has been downward every month, regardless of the
crowing that National members are doing toda y. I say to the members opposite: do not
be too smug. Some of us have been around here long enough to see the crowing rooster
become a feather duster, and that is exactly what we will see from the National Party.

items.speaker: Five wasted years
items.text: 5 long years of delay, of political posturing, and 5 years of weasel
words. Worse still, 5 years of inaction over the Auckland City Rail Link. You know,
National members had it all. It  was given to them, and all th ey had to do was to pick it
up and run. But what did they do? They decided any policy, any good Labour policy,
could not continue, so they turned round and repealed the very mechanism that would
have given them the money to pay for public transport, including rail, in Auckland. It
was a whim. It was a Steven Joyce decision. If it was Labour, it equalled bad. So after 5
wasted years, 5 years of inaction, today they  have been forced by the Labour Party to
accept our policy—to accept a policy that we put in place and started back in the 2000s.
In 2006 we set up the very working party th at decided the future decisions around
rail infrastructure and funding. It included double-tracking of the western commuter rail
line, the redevelopment of the Newmarke t station, the improved linking of Manukau
City to the network, and the electrificati on of rail, and it was around $1 billion that
could be spent. We gave them the mechan ism to pay for the Auckland City Rail Link.

items.speaker: We knew how to pay for it
items.text: a regional fuel tax. It was a mere 10c, and the former mayor
of the North Shore saw immediately that this was a good deal for Auckland—as did all
the other mayors—and signed up to the deal. They signed up and they all agreed. Do
you know that that 10c regional fuel tax, paid by the people of Auckland for their public
transport, would have supported $1.5 billi on in funding that could help pay for the
Auckland rail link?
One of the first things that National di d was to repeal the regional fuel tax—it
repealed the regional fuel tax. But what has happened? It put 9c alone in this last Budget
26 Jun 2013 General Debate 11291
on regional fuel. Nine cents alone, and to  do what? None of it has gone—not just for
Auckland, no.

items.text: No, Dunedin too.

items.text: In Dunedin, in Christchurch, in Wellington—

items.text: Chatham Islands.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: The Chatham Islands—quite right. It has gone everywhere,
and it is doing nothing in terms of public tr ansport. Let me tell you this: National has
not invested in a single public transport infr astructure in Auckla nd since the election.
There have been 5 wasted years.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: What? Not one?

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Not one, not a single one. You know, it is very much of the
1990s. National spent nothing on public transp ort in the 1990s, and then it said: “What
is Labour doing about it?”. Well, we did plenty about it.
Now we are told that National members have always been thinking about it. I have to
tell you that they have been thinking about it in the smallest room in the House. That is
where they have been thinking about it. We ha ve got the biggest U-turn in transport in
living memory. We have gone from no go to get-go. Now they want to invest in it
because they were forced into it by the people of Auckland and by the Labour Party.
And we have the Minister of Transport w ith the biggest egg on his face you have ever
seen. It has taken a whole dozen eggs—scrambled—and there is still not enough egg.
I have to say, where is Nikki Kaye on this, the member for Auckland Central? Why
was she not allowed to speak on a serious issu e? They put up all their clowns to speak
today to crack jokes about polls, but no one got up to say: “We are sorry, Auckland. We
made a mistake. We have wasted 5 years,  and we could have been putting in place
public transport.” It was our policy.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker, for the
opportunity to speak in this general debate. There are a lot of positives that the National
Government has achieved. Heaps of rubbish is being dumped by the Labour Opposition,
which is totally opposite to the facts. I te ll you that the ethnic community does not
believe in Labour Party policies any more.
The New Zealand economy is in better shap e because of the National Government’s
strong, sensible economic management. Our G overnment’s economic plan is to deliver
a faster-growing economy, more jobs, and a re turn to surplus, which remains on track
despite ongoing uncertainty in many parts of the world. The National Government has a
growth-enhancing tax system, with public service and support for science, innovation,
and trade. We recognise that our future  economic performance depends on creating
more new ideas and competing with our global competitors.
For this the funding has risen by 28 percent in the past 4 years. We have made
investment into infrastructure. I am very  much aware, being an Aucklander, how
important it is to improve the general infrastructure in this area in order to expand the
local market. Our Prime Minister, the Rt Hon John Key, is promoting New Zealand as
an outstanding tourist destination. The number  of visitors from overseas visiting all
destinations in New Zeala nd has increased. There has be en $158 million invested to
boost tourism. Not only are tourists bringi ng their tourist dollars but the National
Government is selling to the world more of what our country is producing. We therefore
create more job opportunities for New Zealand businesses to grow, hire more staff, and
invest in the future.
Moreover, more than one-third of the pe ople living in Auckland were born overseas.
The legislation to improve housing affordability will also be very we lcome as this will
speed up the supply of affordable houses to  many migrants within the South Auckland
area. Here I would like to say that we have been fortunate to have Ministers who have
11292 General Debate 26 Jun 2013
been listening. First of all, I would like to  give the example of the Hon Jonathan
Coleman, who brought in the policy for religious  ministers, which wa s one of the main
issues of ethnic communities. Now th e Hon Michael Woodhous e has brought in a
policy for combating the exploitation of migr ant workers, which is also very welcome
to the migrant community.
Here I would like to share the story of ma ny of the migrants who have been coming
to New Zealand to run their own businesses.  While they are competing with others,
some of them are not paying the full minimu m wage. Others are in bad shape, and they
cannot compete with people who are not law-abiding business people. So this policy is a
very good step towards curtailing their unfair advantage over the law-abiding
competitors.
I would also like to share some of the indicators that  show that the economy is
growing. While I was talking to many ta xi drivers during early 2008 and 2009 they
were complaining that they did not have enough business. If we talk to them now, they
say that they are much better off than they  were in 2008. For example, to buy a share in
Auckland Co-op Taxis used to cost about $50,000 a few years ago. Today the price of
that share is more than $100,000. It shows th at the business of th e taxi industry is
growing, which is an indicator that overall the economy is growing.
Another thing that I would like to share with you is that car sales are the highest they
have been in the last 5 years. If we l ook at people’s spending on different things, it
shows that the economy is growing and they have got money to—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: It just shows that the dollar’s too high.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: It is not that the dollar is too high; they have got
money to spend, Mr Mallard. It is important that people have got money in their pocket,
and they want to spend. Thank you.
